A TASTE OF ISRAEL The Negev The Negev is the arid southern half of Israel, running from Be'er Sheva to the Red Sea at Eilat. Nabataean traders once carried incense across it, and David Ben- Gurion saw settling it as essential to the country's future. The sites here range from the copper mines of the Pharaohs to a vast erosion crater, and from desert towns to a coral reef. Eilat Where red mountains meet the blue sea Eilat is Israel's southernmost city, a resort on the Gulf of Aqaba at the head of the Red Sea, with mountains rising on every side and views across to Egypt and Jordan. Its coral reef, the only one in Israel, draws divers and snorkelers all year. Israeli forces reached the site in March 1949, at the end of the War of Independence, and raised the Ink Flag, a hand-drawn Israeli flag, to claim the shore. Eilat has since become both a port and a holiday town. Since 2023 it has also been in range of missiles fired from Yemen, most of them intercepted. Glo

Timna Park Ancient wonders in a surreal landscape Timna Park lies in a desert valley north of Eilat, ringed by red sandstone cliffs and rock formations such as Solomon's Pillars. People mined copper here for thousands of years, and Egyptian expeditions worked the mines more than 3,000 years ago. Rock carvings of chariots, animals, and figures, some of them very old, cover the cliff faces. A reconstructed Egyptian shrine to the goddess Hathor stands near the pillars. Visitors can walk or cycle marked trails, look into ancient mine shafts, and make sand-bottle art at the visitor center. Glossary

Avdat The desert's hidden city and spring Avdat was a Nabataean city on the Incense Route, along which caravans carried frankincense and myrrh from Arabia to the Mediterranean ports. It was named for the Nabataean king Obodas and grew under Roman and Byzantine rule. Its hilltop ruins include a Byzantine church, wine presses, and an acropolis. The city belongs to a UNESCO World Heritage listing for the Incense Route in the Negev. Nearby Ein Avdat canyon has a spring-fed pool and waterfalls among desert cliffs, and local vineyards now revive the ancient wine tradition. Glossary: Avdat

Sde Boker A nation-builder's desert dream Sde Boker is a kibbutz in the heart of the Negev where David Ben-Gurion, Israel's first prime minister, made his home after he left office in 1953. He believed that settling the desert was essential to the country's future and urged young Israelis to do it. His modest hut is preserved as he left it, with his books and study. He and his wife Paula are buried nearby on a clifftop overlooking the Zin canyon. The Midreshet Ben-Gurion campus beside it now holds a research center and a field school. Glossary: Sde Boker

Makhtesh Ramon A crater carved by erosion Makhtesh Ramon is a vast crater in the central Negev, about 40 kilometers long and up to 9 wide. Erosion formed it, not a meteor or a volcano, and its layered walls reveal bands of colored sandstone and fossils. A makhtesh is a landform found only in the Negev and nearby Sinai. Hikers and cyclists follow trails along the rim, ibex wander the cliffs, and the dry, dark sky makes the area popular for stargazing. The town of Mitzpe Ramon sits on the northern edge, where camel rides and a visitor center offer views across the crater. Glossary: Makhtesh Ramo

Be'er Sheva History meets innovation Be'er Sheva, the Negev's largest city, is linked in Genesis to Abraham, who made a covenant with King Abimelech at its well. The modern city grew from an Ottoman administrative town, and in October 1917 British forces and Australian light horsemen took it in a cavalry charge that opened the way into Palestine. The old town still has Ottoman buildings and a railway station. Today the city is a center of technology and education, with Ben-Gurion University and a cyber park, and a Bedouin market where visitors can drink sweet coffee. Glossary: Be'er Sheva

A TASTE OF ISRAEL The Dead Sea The shore of the Dead Sea is the lowest dry land on Earth, more than 400 meters below sea level, and its dry air preserved the scrolls found near Qumran. Oases, fortresses and ancient cities line the shore, from Ein Gedi and Masada to Jericho, and the ruins and salt formations of Sodom tie the Genesis stories to the landscape. The sites here follow the shore and the desert road up to Jerusalem. Dead Sea JORDAN Masada Fortress of freedom and defiance Masada is a rock plateau above the western shore of the Dead Sea. Masada Fortress of freedom and defiance Masada is a rock plateau above the western shore of the Dead Sea. Herod the Great fortified it in the first century BCE as a palace and refuge. During the Jewish revolt against Rome, rebels held it after the fall of Jerusalem in 70 CE. Roman forces besieged it and built a great ramp against its western side. The ancient historian Josephus reports that when the Romans broke in, in 73 or 74 CE, most of the defenders had taken their own lives. Historians debate details of his account. Ein Gedi An oasis of vibrant life in the desert Ein Gedi is an oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea, fed by freshwater springs that run through two canyons, Nahal David and Nahal Arugot. The Hebrew Bible names it as a place where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 24), and the Song of Songs mentions its vineyards. Archaeologists have found a temple from the Chalcolithic period and a Byzantine-era synagogue with a mosaic floor. Qumran Where ancient secrets were unearthed Qumran is an archaeological site on the northwestern shore of the Dead Sea. In 1947 Bedouin shepherds found ancient scrolls in a nearby cave, and later searches turned up manuscripts in eleven caves in all. They include the oldest known copies of books of the Hebrew Bible, as well as texts of a particular community. Many scholars link them to a Jewish group of the Second Temple period, often identified with the Essenes, though that identification is debated. Some of the scrolls are on display in the Shrine of the Book at the Israel Museum in Jerusale

Jericho An ancient city famous for its walls Jericho, near the Jordan River, is among the oldest known inhabited places, with traces of settlement going back about 10,000 years. In the Book of Joshua its walls fell after the Israelites marched around them for seven days, though archaeologists disagree about what the excavated ruins show. Abundant springs have made it an oasis for millennia, and it is known for its dates. Herod the Great built a winter palace nearby. Jericho is administered by the Palestinian Authority and Israelis are barred from entering, so visitors should check current cond

Wadi Qelt A trail through time Wadi Qelt is a desert canyon that carries a stream from the hills near Jerusalem down to Jericho. An ancient road through it linked the two cities, and aqueducts from the Hasmonean and Herodian eras that fed Jericho's palaces and fields can still be seen. St. George's Monastery, a Greek Orthodox monastery founded in the fifth century, clings to the cliff face. Hikers walk the canyon in winter and spring when the stream runs. Parts lie in areas under Palestinian Authority control, and attacks on hikers have occurred, so most go in groups. Glossary: Wadi Qelt

Sodom and Gomorrah Cities of the plain, in tradition and legend According to Genesis, Sodom and Gomorrah were cities of the plain destroyed by fire and brimstone, while Lot and his daughters escaped. Their exact location is unknown, and scholars have proposed sites on both the southern and northern shores of the Dead Sea. A ridge called Mount Sodom, made largely of salt, rises at the southern end of the sea. Its caves and weathered pillars include a formation that visitors call Lot's Wife. The area evokes the story, but no archaeological evidence ties it to the biblical cities. Glossary: Sodom

A TASTE OF ISRAEL Judea and Samaria Judea and Samaria is the hill country between Jerusalem and the Jordan Valley, the setting of much of the Hebrew Bible's narrative. Its sites include the Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron, Shiloh, Beit El, and the twin mountains above Shechem. Israel has held the area since 1967, parts of it are administered by the Palestinian Authority under the Oslo Accords, and its final status is disputed. Hebron City of the Patriarchs, intensely divided Hebron is the traditional burial place of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and their wives, and the Cave of the Patriarchs is sacred to Jews, Christians, and Muslims. Herod built the great enclosure over it, and today it holds both a synagogue and a mosque. A Jewish community lived in Hebron for centuries until riots in 1929, in which 67 Jews were killed and the survivors left. Jews returned after 1967. Bethlehem and Herodium Birthplace of kings, and a palace on a hill Bethlehem, south of Jerusalem, is the traditional birthplace of King David and, in Christian tradition, of Jesus, whose birth the Church of the Nativity marks. The city is administered by the Palestinian Authority and lies behind Israel's security barrier. Nearby, on an artificial hill, are the remains of Herodium, the fortress-palace that Herod the Great built around 20 BCE. Beit El The place of Jacob's ladder Beit El is the biblical site where Jacob dreamed of a ladder reaching to heaven and named the place the house of God (Genesis 28). In the period of the divided kingdom it was a major shrine of the northern kingdom of Israel, and the Bible mentions its altars. Archaeologists have uncovered ancient remains on the ridge, though the exact location of the shrine is debated. Today an Israeli community of the same name stands on the hill, north of Jerusalem, in an area Israel has held since 1967. The status of such communities is disputed. Glossary: Beit El

Shiloh Home of the Tabernacle Shiloh was Israel's chief religious center for much of the period of the judges, about four centuries according to the Bible, and housed the Tabernacle. Hannah prayed here for a child, and her son Samuel grew up serving in its sanctuary (1 Samuel 1). Excavations have found remains of a large Iron Age settlement and of a Byzantine church with mosaics. The site is in Samaria, north of Jerusalem, in an area Israel has administered since 1967. A visitor center offers multimedia exhibits and a view over the ancient mound. Glossary: Shiloh

Mounts Gerizim and Ebal The mountains of blessing and curse Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal stand on either side of the valley at Shechem, the modern city of Nablus. In Deuteronomy and Joshua, the Israelites stood on the two mountains to hear blessings and curses read after crossing the Jordan. Gerizim is the holy mountain of the Samaritans, one of the world's smallest and oldest religious communities, whose few hundred members still hold a Passover sacrifice on its summit. Sebastia Capital of a biblical kingdom Sebastia, in northern Samaria, was the site of ancient Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, which King Omri founded in the ninth century BCE. Herod the Great rebuilt it in Roman style and renamed it Sebaste in honor of Augustus. Visitors can see a Roman forum, a theater, and the foundations of an Israelite royal palace. Later a Crusader cathedral was built over a church said to hold the tomb of John the Baptist. The ruins sit above a village of the same name, in an area administered by the Palestinian Authority. Glossary: Sebastia

Beit She'an Where Rome ruled and empires collided Beit She'an, in the Jordan Valley, was a crossroads of civilizations from the Canaanites onward. In the Bible, the Philistines hung the bodies of King Saul and his sons on its walls (1 Samuel 31). Under Rome it was Scythopolis, the only city of the Decapolis west of the Jordan, and its well-preserved ruins include a theater, bathhouses, and a colonnaded main street. An earthquake in 749 CE brought much of it down, and fallen columns still lie where they fell. The archaeological park is one of the largest in Israel, beside a modern town of the s

Nazareth Childhood home of Jesus, and Israel's largest Arab city Nazareth, in the lower Galilee, is the town where Jesus grew up according to the Gospels, and the Basilica of the Annunciation marks where Christians believe the angel Gabriel told Mary she would bear him. It is also the largest Arab city in Israel, with a Muslim majority, a sizeable Christian minority, and a lively old market. Nearby Upper Nazareth was founded in 1957 as a Jewish town. Pilgrims arrive from around the world, and visitors can try knafeh, a sweet cheese pastry, in the old city. Glossary: Nazareth

Cana Where water was turned to wine Cana is the village where, according to the Gospel of John, Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding, his first miracle. Several places claim the site, but Christian tradition since the Middle Ages has pointed to Kafr Kanna, an Arab town near Nazareth. The Franciscan Wedding Church there displays stone jars said to recall the story, and couples from many countries renew their vows in its chapel. Shops in the town sell wine and olive oil, and the town sits among the hills of the lower Galilee. Glossary: Cana

The Kinneret A lake renowned for miracles of faith The Kinneret, or Sea of Galilee, is Israel's largest freshwater lake, about 21 kilometers long and 13 wide, and it lies some 210 meters below sea level. Its Hebrew name may come from the word for a harp, kinnor, for the lake's shape. The Jordan River feeds it, and it supplies much of Israel's drinking water through the National Water Carrier. The Gospels place miracles on its waters, including Jesus walking on the lake and calming a storm. Tiberias, founded around 20 CE, lies on the western shore, and visitors can take boats across the lake. G

Magdala Home of Mary Magdalene Magdala, on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, was a prosperous fishing town in the first century and is the traditional home of Mary Magdalene. Excavations begun in 2009 uncovered a synagogue from the Second Temple period, one of the oldest found in the Galilee, along with streets, houses, and a market. The Magdala Stone, carved with a seven-branched menorah, was found in the synagogue and is one of the earliest known depictions of the Temple's menorah. The site is now an archaeological park with a modern church beside it. Glossary: Magdala

Capernaum A fishing village at the center of the Gospels Capernaum was a fishing village on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee that the Gospels describe as the center of Jesus's ministry. He is said to have taught in its synagogue and healed the sick there, and the home of the apostle Peter was here. Excavations have uncovered a fourth or fifth century limestone synagogue built over an earlier basalt one, and the remains of a house that a modern church now covers. The village was abandoned around the 11th century and was rediscovered by archaeologists in the 19th. Glossary: Capernaum

Mount of Beatitudes Site of the Sermon on the Mount The Mount of Beatitudes is a hillside above the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee, traditionally identified as the place where Jesus delivered the Sermon on the Mount, which opens with the Beatitudes (Matthew 5). The identification dates to the Byzantine period, and the present octagonal church was built in the 1930s. Its gardens and terraces look out over the lake and the hills of the Galilee, and the quiet setting draws pilgrims and walkers. The exact place of the sermon is not known. Glossary: Mount of Beatitudes

Safed City of mysticism and the center of Kabbalah Safed, high in the Upper Galilee, is one of Judaism's four holy cities and the center of Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition. After the expulsion from Spain in 1492 many scholars and mystics settled there, among them Isaac Luria, known as the Ari, and Joseph Karo, who wrote the Shulchan Aruch. The Ari Synagogue and the cobbled lanes of the old Jewish quarter preserve that period. Today Safed is also an artists' colony, with galleries in the Artists' Quarter, and a summer retreat for its cool mountain air. Glossary: Safed (Tzfat)

Hula Valley Paradise for birds and bird lovers The Hula Valley in the northern Galilee is a wetland on one of the great bird migration routes between Europe, Asia, and Africa. Each autumn tens of thousands of cranes stop here, along with pelicans, storks, and many other species, and the passage over Israel is estimated at hundreds of millions of birds a year. The valley's marshes were drained in the 1950s to fight malaria and create farmland, and part of the area was later reflooded to restore the ecosystem and create the Agamon Hula park. Visitors can rent bicycles for the paths. Glossary: Hu

A TASTE OF ISRAEL The Golan Heights The Golan Heights is a volcanic plateau rising from the Sea of Galilee to Mount Hermon, Israel's highest peak. Israel captured it from Syria in 1967 and applied Israeli law there in 1981, a step the United States recognized in 2019 but most other countries have not. The sites here include ancient synagogues, vineyards, and the battlefields of 1967 and 1973. Gamla The Masada of the north Gamla was a Jewish town on a steep ridge in the Golan, shaped like a camel's hump, from which its name derives. In 67 CE it held out against Roman forces in the Jewish revolt, and according to Josephus thousands of its people died when the town fell, many by throwing themselves off the cliff. Excavations have uncovered a synagogue from the first century, one of the oldest known, along with a city wall, houses, and a ritual bath. The nature reserve around it has a high waterfall and a colony of griffon vultures that nest in the cliffs. Glossary: Gamla

Katzrin Life in the Talmudic era Katzrin was a village of the Talmudic era in the central Golan, inhabited from about the fourth to the eighth centuries, with a synagogue, houses, and an olive press. A partial reconstruction shows how its people lived, with stone homes and a working press, and there are demonstrations of bread baking and grain grinding. The archaeological park sits beside the modern town of Katzrin, founded in 1977, which serves as a regional center for the Golan. Nearby are a winery and a museum of Golan antiquities, which displays finds from many ancient synagogues. Glossary

Valley of Tears A battlefield remembered The Valley of Tears, in the northern Golan, was the scene of fierce tank fighting in the first days of the Yom Kippur War in October 1973. Syria attacked with several divisions, and outnumbered Israeli armored brigades held the line for days until reserves arrived. Hundreds of Israeli soldiers died in the battle for the Golan, and a memorial on the hillside honors those who fell. Burnt-out tanks remain along the road, and a museum recounts the battle through the accounts of those who fought. Glossary: Valley of Tears

Quneitra Viewpoint A window onto a tank-strewn battlefield At the Quneitra viewpoint, near the Israeli border, visitors can look down on the abandoned Syrian town of Quneitra. Israel captured the town in 1967 and withdrew from it under the 1974 disengagement agreement that followed the Yom Kippur War. The town was heavily damaged, and Syria and Israel blame each other for that. A UN observer force, UNDOF, has patrolled a buffer zone along the line since 1974. Since the Syrian civil war began in 2011 the area has seen fighting among several groups, and the border is closely watched. Glossary: Q

Banias Sacred springs and ancient shrines Banias, at the foot of Mount Hermon, is one of the main sources of the Jordan River. A spring flows from a cave once sacred to the Greek god Pan, from which the name Paneas, later Banias, derives. Herod built a temple to Augustus here, and the city became a regional center, with a Roman bathhouse and a palace. The Gospels place a conversation between Jesus and his disciples nearby, at Caesarea Philippi. A short trail leads to a waterfall, and the nature reserve has riverside paths and a Crusader fortress above. Glossary: Banias

Mount Hermon The roof and eyes of Israel At 2,236 meters, Mount Hermon is the highest peak in the Israeli-held part of a range that straddles the borders of Israel, Syria, and Lebanon. Its snow feeds the headwaters of the Jordan River, and in winter it hosts Israel's only ski resort. Israel took the southern slopes in the Six-Day War of 1967, and an Israeli intelligence outpost on the summit became known as the Eyes of the Nation. The Hebrew Bible mentions the mountain several times. In summer, a chairlift and trails offer cool air and views toward Syria and Lebanon. Glossary: Mount Hermon

A TASTE OF ISRAEL The Mediterranean Coast The Mediterranean coast runs from the white cliffs of Rosh Hanikra at the Lebanese border south to Herzliya, taking in the Carmel ridge, the port cities of Akko and Haifa, Herod's harbor at Caesarea, and the Crusader ruins at Apollonia. Border communities in the far north were evacuated after rocket and missile fire from Lebanon began in October 2023. Near Netanya the country was only about 15 kilometers wide before 1967, which has shaped its security thinking ever since. Rosh Hanikra Where the sea meets the cliffs Rosh Hanikra is a chalk cliff on the Mediterranean at Israel's border with Lebanon, where the sea has carved caves and grottos into the rock. A short, steep cable car carries visitors down to the grottos. British forces built a railway tunnel here in 1942, during World War II, to link Haifa with Beirut and Tripoli, and the line was closed in 1948. The site lies in an area that has been under fire from Lebanon since October 2023, and the cable car and grottos have been closed at times, so visitors should check current conditions. Glossary: Rosh Hanikr

Akko A Crusader stronghold and Ottoman gem Akko, or Acre, is an ancient port on the northern edge of Haifa Bay. Its old city, a UNESCO World Heritage site, preserves the Crusader capital of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, with underground halls of the Knights Hospitaller, and Ottoman-era walls, mosques, and a covered market. Napoleon failed to take the city in 1799, after a siege of about two months. Today Akko has a mixed population of Arabs and Jews, a working fishing harbor, and restaurants known for fresh fish. Glossary: Akko (Acre)

Haifa A city of coexistence and innovation Haifa, Israel's third-largest city, climbs the slopes of Mount Carmel above a large natural bay and a major port. It is known for its relatively easy relations among Jewish, Arab, Christian, Muslim, Druze, and Bahá'í residents, and for the Technion, Israel's institute of technology. The Bahá'í Gardens, nineteen terraces descending the mountain around the golden-domed Shrine of the Báb, are a UNESCO World Heritage site. The German Colony at the foot of the hill was built by Templers in the 19th century and now holds restaurants and cafes. Glossary: Hai

Mount Carmel Biblical history and natural beauty Mount Carmel is a coastal mountain ridge that rises beside Haifa. In the Book of Kings, the prophet Elijah challenged the priests of Baal here to prove whose god was true, and fire from heaven consumed his offering (1 Kings 18). The Muhraka Carmelite monastery commemorates the event, and its roof offers a wide view of the Jezreel Valley. The Carmel National Park has trails through oak woods, and the caves of Nahal Me'arot, where prehistoric human remains were found, are a UNESCO World Heritage site. Glossary: Mount Carmel

Atlit A detention camp and a daring rescue Atlit, south of Haifa, is the site of a British detention camp used from 1939 to 1948 to hold Jews who tried to enter Mandate Palestine without permits. Many were survivors of the Holocaust. In October 1945 the Palmach raided the camp at night and freed about 200 detainees. The preserved barracks and a refitted immigrant ship are now a museum. Leon Uris set part of his novel Exodus here, and the camp has become a symbol of the struggle over Jewish immigration under the British Mandate. Glossary: Atlit

Caesarea Roman splendor on the sea Caesarea was built by Herod the Great between 25 and 13 BCE and named for the Roman emperor Augustus. Its artificial harbor, a feat of ancient engineering, made it the main port of Judea, and under Roman rule it was the seat of the provincial governor, Pontius Pilate among them. Visitors can see a Roman theater that hosts concerts again, a hippodrome, and an aqueduct that carried water from springs miles away. Crusaders later fortified the town, and their walls and moat stand beside the harbor. Glossary: Caesarea

Netanya Seaside city of relaxation and resilience Netanya, on the central coast, was founded in 1929 and named for the American Jewish philanthropist Nathan Straus. It grew with waves of immigrants, and its beaches and seaside promenade made it a popular resort, sometimes called the Israeli Riviera, with many French and Russian speakers among its residents. On March 27, 2002, a suicide bomber killed 30 people at a Passover seder at the Park Hotel, one of the deadliest attacks of the Second Intifada. The city has since been rebuilt and the hotel restored. Glossary: Netanya

Apollonia Cliffs, Crusaders, and Phoenician roots Apollonia-Arsuf, on a sandstone cliff north of Herzliya, was a harbor in the Phoenician and Persian periods before the Greeks named it for Apollo. The Arabs called it Arsuf, a name the Crusaders kept. In 1191 Richard the Lionheart defeated Saladin in the Battle of Arsuf nearby. The Crusaders fortified the town, but the Mamluk sultan Baybars destroyed it in 1265. The national park preserves the castle and moat, a Roman villa, and sweeping views of the sea. Glossary: Apollonia (Arsuf)

Herzliya The heart of Israel's Silicon Wadi Herzliya, named for Theodor Herzl, the founder of political Zionism, was founded in 1924 and grew from a farming village into one of Israel's wealthiest cities. Its Herzliya Pituach district is home to many technology and biotech companies, and the area is sometimes called Silicon Wadi. A marina, beaches, and luxury hotels line the coast. Herzl's slogan, "If you will it, it is no dream," gives the city a motto for ambitious plans. The annual Herzliya Conference is an important gathering on Israeli security and policy. Glossary: Herzliya

A TASTE OF ISRAEL Tel Aviv and Jaffa Jaffa is one of the world's oldest ports, and Tel Aviv began in 1909 as a neighborhood of Jaffa built on sand dunes. The two were merged into one municipality in 1950 and now share a shoreline of beaches, markets, and Bauhaus buildings recognized by UNESCO. The sites here run from the old harbor north along the sea and into the city where Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated in 1995. Neve Tzedek Where Tel Aviv began Neve Tzedek, founded in 1887, was the first Jewish neighborhood built outside Jaffa, and it is where the story of Tel Aviv begins. Its low houses with shutters and courtyards decayed in the 20th century and were restored from the 1980s on. Today it is one of the city's most fashionable quarters, with boutiques, galleries, and cafes. The Suzanne Dellal Center for Dance and Theatre, in a former school, is home to the Batsheva Dance Company, and the writer S. Y. Agnon once lived here. Glossary: Neve Tzedek

Rothschild Boulevard The beating heart of Tel Aviv culture Rothschild Boulevard is a tree-lined avenue through the center of Tel Aviv, laid out in the early days of the city, which was founded in 1909 on sand dunes north of Jaffa. At number 16, Independence Hall is where David Ben-Gurion read the Declaration of the State of Israel on May 14, 1948. The surrounding White City, with some 4,000 Bauhaus and International- style buildings of the 1930s, is a UNESCO World Heritage site. Cafes and kiosks line the central path, and the boulevard has become a symbol of the city's cultural life. Glossary:

Carmel Market A cheap feast for the senses The Carmel Market, known in Hebrew as Shuk HaCarmel, is Tel Aviv's largest open-air market, and it has run along a street in the city center since the 1920s. Stalls sell fruit, vegetables, spices, fish, cheese, bread, and flowers, and vendors call out prices in Hebrew, Arabic, and other languages. Street food stands serve falafel, shakshuka, and halva, and food tours are popular. On Fridays before the Sabbath the lanes fill with shoppers, and the nearby Nahalat Binyamin craft fair on Tuesdays and Fridays draws more. Glossary: Carmel Market

Rabin Square A plaza of democracy and remembrance Rabin Square, in front of Tel Aviv's city hall, was called Kings of Israel Square until 1995. On November 4 of that year, at the end of a rally in support of the peace process, Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin was shot dead there by Yigal Amir, a Jewish extremist who opposed the Oslo Accords. A memorial marks the spot. The square remains the city's main gathering place for demonstrations, concerts, and public ceremonies, and many Israelis return each year on the anniversary of the assassination. Glossary: Rabin (Kings of Israel) Square

Sarona Market and Hostage Square A restored colony and a place of waiting Sarona was founded in 1871 as a colony by German Templers, a Protestant movement, and its red-roofed houses, restored in the 2000s, now form a district of restaurants, shops, and a large food market. Beside it stands the Kirya, the military headquarters complex. After Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023 and took about 250 people hostage into Gaza, a nearby plaza became known as Hostage Square, a gathering place for families and supporters during the long effort to bring them home. Glossary: Sarona Market and Hostage

A TASTE OF ISRAEL The Judean Hills The Judean Hills west of Jerusalem carry the road that Israel's forces fought to open during the siege of the city in 1948. Latrun, the Castel, and the Burma Road mark that struggle, while Ein Kerem, Sataf, and Abu Ghosh show village life and ancient farming terraces. The sites here lie on the approaches to Jerusalem. Latrun Battles and bravery Latrun is a hilltop overlooking the main road from the coast to Jerusalem, where the Trappist Monastery of Latrun, founded in the 1890s, still makes wine and olive oil. Latrun Battles and bravery Latrun is a hilltop overlooking the main road from the coast to Jerusalem, where the Trappist Monastery of Latrun, founded in the 1890s, still makes wine and olive oil. In May and June 1948, Israeli forces tried several times to take the Jordanian-held Latrun fortress to open the road to besieged Jerusalem, and failed with heavy losses. Latrun stayed in Jordanian hands until the Six-Day War in 1967. The museum at Yad La-Shiryon tells the story of Israel's Armored Corps, with tanks displayed outdoors. Glossary: Latrun

Burma Road A lifeline to Jerusalem The Burma Road was a rough bypass built in May and June 1948 to carry supplies to Jerusalem, which Jordanian forces at Latrun had cut off from the coast. Engineers and volunteers cut a track through the hills, and porters hauled loads along it before the road was ready. It opened on June 10, in time to relieve the city before a truce. It was named after the wartime Burma Road to China. Parts have been restored, and a trail now follows it, with a monument at the Jerusalem end. Glossary: Burma Road

Abu Ghosh A village of harmony and prosperity Abu Ghosh is a village of about 7,000 residents just west of Jerusalem, known for its restaurants serving hummus and for its cooperation with Jewish neighbors. During the 1948 war its leaders stayed on good terms with nearby Jewish communities, and the villagers were not expelled. The village is home to a Crusader church, built in the 12th century and now used by Benedictine monks, whose acoustics make it a venue for an annual choral music festival. Its residents are mostly Muslim, with a small Christian minority. Glossary: Abu Ghosh

Castel National Park Conquering the high ground The Castel is a hilltop with a Crusader fortress above the road to Jerusalem, beside the site of the Arab village of al-Qastal. Control of it changed hands several times in April 1948, during Operation Nachshon, when Haganah and Palmach forces fought to open the road, and the Arab commander Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni was killed in the fighting. The park preserves trenches, a memorial, and the Crusader ruins, and offers a view over the Jerusalem corridor. Glossary: Castel National Park

Sataf Ancient agriculture revived Sataf is a nature reserve in the Jerusalem hills where terraced hillsides and a spring-fed irrigation system recall farming that goes back to biblical times. Arab villagers cultivated the terraces until 1948, and Israeli volunteers restored them in recent decades. Visitors can walk through terraced gardens planted with olive, fig, and grape, and a small organic farm sells produce. Trails lead to the spring and through the forest, and the site is a favorite for family picnics. Archaeological remains include a tunnel and a pool. Glossary: Sataf

Ein Kerem A village of beauty and spirituality Ein Kerem, now a Jerusalem neighborhood in a green valley, is traditionally the birthplace of John the Baptist, and the Church of St. John the Baptist and the Church of the Visitation mark the events. Mary's Spring, where villagers drew water for centuries, lies at the center. Until 1948 it was an Arab village, and after the war Jewish immigrants and later artists moved into the old stone houses. Today its alleys hold galleries and restaurants, and the Hadassah Medical Center, with Marc Chagall's stained-glass windows, stands on the hill above. Gl

A TASTE OF ISRAEL Jerusalem Jerusalem is Israel's capital and a holy city for Jews, Christians, and Muslims, whose most sacred places stand within a few hundred meters of each other. Israel took the Old City in 1967 and later annexed East Jerusalem, a step most countries do not recognize and the Palestinians contest. The sites here run from the Temple Mount and the Western Wall through the City of David and the markets to the national museums and Yad Vashem. The Temple Mount Holiest site in Judaism, third holiest in Islam The Temple Mount is a walled plateau in the Old City, the holiest site in Judaism, where the First Temple, built by Solomon, and the Second Temple, expanded by Herod, once stood. It is also the third holiest site in Islam, known as al-Haram al-Sharif, and is crowned by the Dome of the Rock, completed in 691, and the Al-Aqsa Mosque. Israel has controlled the area since 1967, while a Muslim religious trust, the Waqf, manages the compound. Jews may visit but not pray there, and its status is among the most disputed questions in the

The Western Wall and Tunnels A remnant of the Temple platform The Western Wall, or Kotel, is a surviving section of the retaining wall of the Second Temple's platform, and it is the holiest place where Jews are permitted to pray. Jews were barred from it under Jordanian rule from 1948 to 1967, and after Israel captured the Old City in the Six-Day War the plaza was cleared and opened. Separate sections serve men and women. Beneath neighboring buildings, the Western Wall Tunnels reveal the length of the wall, including a stone weighing about 570 tons, an ancient aqueduct, and Roman and Herodian

The City of David Jerusalem's beginnings are tied to water The City of David is the narrow ridge south of the Temple Mount where the earliest settlement of Jerusalem stood, and according to the Bible King David made it his capital about 3,000 years ago. Excavations since the 19th century have uncovered Bronze and Iron Age walls, a stepped stone structure, and a royal-era building. Hezekiah's Tunnel, a water channel dug around 700 BCE ahead of an Assyrian siege, leads visitors through knee-deep water to the Pool of Siloam. The site lies in the Palestinian neighborhood of Silwan, and the excavat

Mount Zion The hill that gave Zionism its name Mount Zion is the hill just south of the Old City walls, and its name has come to stand for Jerusalem and for the longing of the Jewish people for the land. Tradition places here the Tomb of King David, though scholars doubt it, and the Room of the Last Supper, called the Cenacle. The Dormition Abbey, a German Benedictine church completed in 1910, commemorates the falling asleep of the Virgin Mary. A Christian cemetery on the slope holds the grave of Oskar Schindler. Glossary: Mount Zion

The Mount of Olives and Gethsemane A panoramic view of history The Mount of Olives is the ridge east of the Old City, with a sweeping view over the Temple Mount. Its slopes hold the oldest and most important Jewish cemetery, in use for some 3,000 years, as well as Christian churches and a Russian Orthodox convent. Jews could not visit the cemetery between 1948 and 1967. At the foot of the ridge, the Garden of Gethsemane is where, in the Gospels, Jesus prayed before his arrest, and its ancient olive trees are among the oldest in the region. The Church of All Nations stands beside it. Glossary:

Mea She'arim Step back a century or two Mea She'arim is a neighborhood north of the Old City, founded in 1874, and its name means a hundred gates, after a verse in Genesis. Its crowded lanes, small synagogues, and study halls are home to ultra-Orthodox Jews, many of whom dress as their ancestors did in Eastern Europe. Signs ask visitors to dress modestly and not to photograph residents. The community has long disagreed with secular Israelis over Sabbath observance and over military service, which remains a continuing political dispute. Glossary: Mea She'arim

Mahane Yehuda Market The bustling tastes of Jerusalem Mahane Yehuda, known as the Shuk, is Jerusalem's main open-air market, founded in the late 19th century. Its lanes hold stalls with produce, spices, baked goods, halva, and cheese, and vendors call out prices in a mix of languages. By night, bars and restaurants fill the alleys and attract a younger crowd. The market has been the target of terror attacks, notably on July 30, 1997, when two suicide bombers killed 16 people and wounded 178. It draws shoppers and visitors in large numbers, especially before the Sabbath. Glossary: Mahane Yehuda

x: The Israel Museum and Shrine of the Book Art, archaeology, and the scrolls The Israel Museum, founded in 1965, is Israel's national museum, with archaeology, Judaica, fine art, and a sculpture garden designed by Isamu Noguchi. Its Shrine of the Book, a white dome shaped like the lid of a jar that held the Dead Sea Scrolls, houses scrolls found at Qumran and elsewhere. The museum also has a large model of Jerusalem as it looked in the Second Temple period. Visitors can follow the story of the land from prehistory to contemporary art in a single hilltop campus. Glossary: Israel Museum and Shrine

Yad Vashem Remembrance of the Six Million Yad Vashem, on the Mount of Remembrance in Jerusalem, is Israel's national Holocaust memorial and research center, established by law in 1953. Its history museum tells the story of the destruction of European Jewry through documents, objects, and testimony, and its Hall of Names records the six million Jews who were murdered. A memorial to the 1.5 million children who died, an Avenue of the Righteous Among the Nations honoring non-Jews who rescued Jews, and a research institute and archive complete the campus. A TASTE OF ISRAEL The Southern Plain (Shfela) This chapter covers the low country south of Tel Aviv down to the Gaza border. Its sites include the Philistine cities of Ashkelon and Ashdod, the farming town of Rishon LeZion, and Yavne, where rabbinic scholarship was rebuilt after the destruction of the Temple. The chapter ends at the Gaza border, where Israel withdrew in 2005 and Hamas attacked communities and a music festival on October 7, 2023. Mediterranean Sea Rishon LeZion City of pioneers Rishon LeZion, "First to Zion," was founded in 1882 by Jewish immigrants from Russia and became a mod

Rishon LeZion City of pioneers Rishon LeZion, "First to Zion," was founded in 1882 by Jewish immigrants from Russia and became a model for later farming settlements, with the backing of Baron Edmond de Rothschild. Its vineyards and wine cellars made it a center of Israel's early wine industry, and a school that opened there in 1886 was among the first to teach in Hebrew. Today Rishon is one of Israel's largest cities, and its museum and old wine cellars recall the pioneers. It lies on the coastal plain just south of Tel Aviv. Glossary: Rishon LeZion

Yavne The birthplace of Rabbinic Judaism Yavne, on the coastal plain south of Tel Aviv, became a center of Jewish learning after the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE. According to the Talmud, Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, who had left besieged Jerusalem, asked the Roman commander Vespasian for permission to found a school here, and the Sanhedrin met in Yavne. Rabbinic Judaism, centered on study and prayer, took shape in this period. Excavations have found a large Byzantine-era winemaking complex and other ancient remains, and Yavne is today a growing modern city. Glossary: Yavne

Ashdod A city of ancient and modern import Ashdod was one of the five cities of the Philistines, and the Bible tells of the Ark of the Covenant being brought to its temple of the god Dagon after a battle with the Israelites (1 Samuel 5). Modern Ashdod, founded in 1956, is a port city that handles much of Israel's seaborne cargo and has grown into one of its largest cities. The Mamane Museum shows finds from the Philistine period, and a long promenade runs along the beach. The city has been under rocket fire from Gaza many times in recent decades. Glossary: Ashdod

Ashkelon A gateway to the Mediterranean Ashkelon was a major Canaanite and Philistine port, and its mound has yielded some of the best-known finds of that era, including an early arched gate, a silver calf figurine, and a Philistine cemetery. The city later passed through Greek, Roman, Byzantine, and Crusader hands, and Saladin ordered its walls destroyed in 1191. Today the national park on the beach holds the ruins along with the remains of a Roman council house and columns, and the modern city lies just north. Glossary: Ashkelon

Ofakim A town of transformation Ofakim, in the northern Negev, was founded in the 1950s as a development town for new immigrants, many of them Jews from North Africa and Asia. It grew with farms and small factories, and an annual pomegranate festival celebrates local agriculture. On October 7, 2023, Hamas gunmen entered the town, and residents were held in their homes for many hours before Israeli forces cleared the area. The town has since worked to recover, and it remains a quiet place, a few kilometers from the Gaza border region. Glossary: Ofakim

Sderot Surviving despite adversity and attack Sderot, about a kilometer from the Gaza Strip, was founded in 1951 as a town for immigrants, many of them from Morocco and Iran. Since 2001 it has been the target of rocket and mortar fire from Gaza, and many public places have shelters or fortified bus stops. Residents and artists have responded with local music, theater, and an arts scene, and an underground concert hall has been built. On October 7, 2023, Hamas gunmen killed dozens of residents and soldiers in and around the town. Glossary: Sderot

The Gaza Border Kibbutzim Communal life on the frontline Kibbutzim are collective communities, and about twenty communities of the Gaza border region, among them Be'eri, Kfar Aza, Nir Oz, and Nahal Oz, lie within a few kilometers of the fence. Many of their members worked for years for better relations with Gaza, and some volunteered to drive Gazan patients to Israeli hospitals. Israel withdrew from Gaza in 2005, and Hamas took power in 2007. On October 7, 2023, Hamas-led gunmen broke through the border and attacked the kibbutzim, killing hundreds of residents and taking many hostage. Glossary

Re'im Site of the Nova festival Re'im is a kibbutz near the Gaza border, and next to it a field hosted the Nova music festival, an all-night dance gathering, on October 6 and 7, 2023. At dawn on October 7, Hamas-led gunmen attacked the festival, and according to Israeli figures more than 360 people were killed and about 40 were taken hostage. The attackers also overran a nearby army base. The festival grounds, with the remains of the stage and burned cars, are now a memorial site, with photographs of those who died. Glossary: Re'im

Gaza (Gush Katif) A land of ancient memory and recent war The Gaza Strip lies between Israel and Egypt, in the region of the ancient Philistine city of Gaza, where the Bible places the death of Samson. Israel captured it from Egypt in 1967, and from the 1970s Israeli settlers built a bloc of communities in its southwest called Gush Katif, with about 9,000 residents in 21 settlements. In August 2005 Israel withdrew all its settlers and troops under the Disengagement Plan. Hamas won elections in 2006 and took full control in 2007. Israelis still disagree about whether the withdrawal was necessar

FLORA AND FAUNA Trees of Israel Israel's trees range from ancient olives and great oaks of the north to flat-topped acacias in the southern desert. Some are native, some were planted by early settlers, and some appear in the Bible. Rainfall shapes the pattern. The wetter north and the hills support woods of oak, carob, and terebinth, the dry south holds only hardy trees that can reach deep water, and irrigation has made palm groves possible in the hot valleys. In the 20th century, foresters planted pines and eucalyptus on bare hills, and today more native species are being used again. Many old

Carob The tree of the sweet pod חרובCeratonia siliqua The carob is a dark evergreen with glossy leaves and long brown pods that taste faintly of chocolate. It grows wild on hillsides across the country and is planted in gardens and along roads. Its pods were long used as animal fodder and as a sweetener, and carob syrup is still sold in markets. The tree grows slowly and can live for centuries. A story in the Talmud tells of an old man planting a carob he would never see bear fruit, so that his grandchildren could eat from it. Glossary: Carob

Olive A tree that outlives its planters זיתOlea europaea Olive trees have grown in the land for thousands of years, and some groves are said to be centuries old. Their silver-green leaves and twisted trunks are a familiar sight in the Galilee, the Judean hills, and Samaria. The olives are picked in autumn and pressed into oil, which has been a staple of local cooking and trade since ancient times. Two olive branches also frame the menorah on the emblem of the State of Israel, a sign of peace. Glossary: Olive

Tabor oak The great oak of the Galilee אלון התבורQuercus ithaburensis The Tabor oak is a broad, deciduous oak of the Galilee, the Golan, and the Carmel, named for Mount Tabor in the lower Galilee. It sheds its leaves in winter and grows large, with a wide crown that gives deep shade. Many stand alone in open fields, spared by farmers over the centuries and treasured by villages as shade and meeting places. Its acorns have large, scaly caps. Old oaks are protected, and some in the north are among the largest trees in the country. Glossary: Tabor oak

Atlantic terebinth A sacred tree on the hilltop אלה אטלנטיתPistacia atlantica The Atlantic terebinth is a large, slow-growing tree, often seen alone on a hilltop or beside a tomb. Local communities have long treated such trees as holy, and visitors sometimes tie strips of cloth to the branches. The Hebrew name ela appears in the Bible, and the Valley of Elah, where David is said to have fought Goliath, is named after the tree. It can live for hundreds of years, and its small red berries are eaten by birds. Glossary: Atlantic terebinth

Date palm A symbol of the land תמרPhoenix dactylifera The date palm grows in the Jordan Valley, the Arava, and the oases of the Dead Sea, where the heat and irrigation suit it. Israel exports large quantities of dates, among them the sweet Medjool variety. Ancient Judean coins show the palm, and the Bible links it to abundance. In 2005, scientists at Kibbutz Ketura sprouted a date palm from a seed about 2,000 years old that was found at Masada. The tree, nicknamed Methuselah, has since grown and flowered. Glossary: Date palm

Tamarisk Hardy shade for salt and sun אשלTamarix The tamarisk is a feathery tree that survives where few others do. It tolerates salt, heat, and poor soil, and it pushes salt out through its leaves, leaving a pale crust. It grows along streambeds and the desert edge, and farmers plant it as a windbreak. According to Genesis, Abraham planted an eshel, a tamarisk, at Be'er Sheva and called there on the name of God. Tamarisks still shade parks and yards in the city today. Glossary: Tamarisk

Aleppo pine The common forest tree אורן ירושלמיPinus halepensis The Aleppo pine is the most widely planted forest tree in Israel. It also grows wild in places such as the Jerusalem hills and the Carmel. It grows fast, tolerates thin, rocky soil, and gives a light shade. Foresters planted it in great numbers during the 20th century to cover bare hills. Its needles and resin burn easily, however, and forest fires are a recurring danger in dry summers. Newer plantings use a wider mix of trees, including oaks and carobs. Glossary: Aleppo pine

Acacia Flat-topped tree of the desert שיטהVachellia Acacias are thorny, umbrella-shaped trees of the Negev and the Arava. Their deep roots reach water far below the surface, and their shade shelters gazelles, ibex, and desert birds. Camels and goats eat the pods. The Hebrew name shita appears in the Bible, where shittim wood is used to build the Tabernacle, and the wood is hard and resistant to decay. Many acacias in the south are protected, and some have survived for generations in dry riverbeds. Glossary: Acacia

Eucalyptus An Australian import אקליפטוסEucalyptus Eucalyptus trees are not native. Settlers brought them from Australia in the 19th century and planted them in swampy areas, because the trees drink large amounts of water and helped dry out the marshes where malaria spread. Tall, with peeling bark and a sharp scent, they now line roads and farm edges and shade many villages and kibbutzim. They are also planted as windbreaks. Their dense roots can be a problem for other plants, and some are now being replaced with native trees. Glossary: Eucalyptus

FLORA AND FAUNA Wildflowers The winter rains turn the hills green, and from December to April wildflowers cover much of the country. Many species are protected, and picking them is against the law. These six are among the best known. Red anemone Red carpets of winter כלניתAnemone coronaria The red anemone, kalanit in Hebrew, carpets hillsides, fields, and roadsides from December to March. It is the best-known wildflower of the Israeli winter, and crowds visit the fields where it grows. Every year, a festival called Darom Adom, Red South, marks its bloom in the northwestern Negev. The flowers o

Red anemone Red carpets of winter כלניתAnemone coronaria The red anemone, kalanit in Hebrew, carpets hillsides, fields, and roadsides from December to March. It is the best-known wildflower of the Israeli winter, and crowds visit the fields where it grows. Every year, a festival called Darom Adom, Red South, marks its bloom in the northwestern Negev. The flowers open in sunshine and close at night or in rain. Wild anemones can also be white, pink, or purple, though red is by far the most common. Picking them is forbidden. Glossary: Red anemone

Cyclamen Pink blooms from the rocks רקפתCyclamen persicum The cyclamen, raqefet in Hebrew, grows from rocky crevices in the hills of the Galilee, the Carmel, and Judea. Its pink or white flowers appear from November to March, held above heart-shaped leaves with silver patterns. After blooming, the stem curls down and pulls the seed pod toward the ground. Ants then carry the seeds away. It is protected, but cultivated cyclamens are widely sold as pot plants, and many Israelis plant them in winter window boxes. Glossary: Cyclamen

Sea daffodil A white star on the dunes חבצלת החוףPancratium maritimum The sea daffodil, a white, sweet-smelling flower, blooms on coastal sand dunes in late summer, at a time when most other flowers have faded. It grows from a deep bulb and survives heat, salt spray, and shifting sand. Coastal building has destroyed many of its habitats, and the flower is now protected. Its Hebrew name recalls the chavatzelet of the Song of Songs, though scholars disagree about which plant that verse describes. Visitors may still find it on beaches in August and September. Glossary: Sea daffodil

Gilboa iris A rare purple iris אירוס הגלבועIris haynei The Gilboa iris is a large, deep purple flower that grows wild on Mount Gilboa, in the north of the country, and almost nowhere else. It blooms for only a few weeks, in February and March, and hundreds of visitors travel to the ridge each spring to see it. The mountain is also named in the Bible, in David's lament for Saul and Jonathan. The iris is protected, and the Nature and Parks Authority has marked paths so that visitors do not trample the plants. Glossary: Gilboa iris

Poppy Fields of red פרגPapaver In March and April, wild poppies spread across fields, roadsides, and empty lots, often next to yellow crown daisies. Their paper-thin petals fall within a day or two of opening, but new blooms replace them for weeks. They thrive in disturbed soil, so they grow thickly beside plowed fields and new roads. Poppies are common in Europe as well, and in much of the world they are worn as a flower of remembrance. In Israel they simply mark the arrival of spring. Glossary: Poppy

Narcissus Fragrance in the winter fields נרקיס מצויNarcissus tazetta The narcissus, a small white flower with a yellow cup at its center, grows in damp fields and valleys during the winter months. Several flowers bloom together on one stem, and their strong sweet scent can be noticed from a distance. The plant grows from a bulb and spreads in clusters. Its scent has been used in perfumes for centuries. It is a protected species, and groups of walkers often search for it on winter hikes in the Galilee and along the coastal plain. Glossary: Narcissus

FLORA AND FAUNA Wildlife Israel's animals come from Europe, Africa, and Asia, and several nearly disappeared before being brought back by reintroduction programs. Some are common sights and others are rarely seen, but all of them live within a short drive of the country's cities. Nubian ibex Sure-footed on the cliffs יעלCapra nubiana The Nubian ibex is a wild goat with long, curved horns, and it lives on desert cliffs and canyon walls. It is easily seen at Ein Gedi, Makhtesh Ramon, and Sde Boker, where herds come to drink at dusk. Males have heavy horns that can reach more than a meter. The Bi

Nubian ibex Sure-footed on the cliffs יעלCapra nubiana The Nubian ibex is a wild goat with long, curved horns, and it lives on desert cliffs and canyon walls. It is easily seen at Ein Gedi, Makhtesh Ramon, and Sde Boker, where herds come to drink at dusk. Males have heavy horns that can reach more than a meter. The Bible mentions the ya'el in the Psalms as an animal that finds safety in the high rocks. Ibex are protected, and visitors should keep their distance and not feed them. Glossary: Nubian ibex

Rock hyrax A small cousin of the elephant שפן סלעProcavia capensis The rock hyrax is a furry, rabbit-sized animal that lives in colonies among the rocks, and it is easy to see at Ein Gedi and in the Judean desert. Despite its look, its closest living relatives are elephants and manatees. Hyraxes sunbathe in groups, with one standing guard and calling out when an eagle or a snake appears. The Bible names the shafan as an animal that makes its home among the rocks, and listed it in its dietary laws. Glossary: Rock hyrax

Mountain gazelle Graceful in the hills צבי ארץ ישראליGazella gazella The mountain gazelle is a slender, light brown antelope that lives in the hills and on the coastal plain. Its Hebrew name, tzvi, also means beauty or glory, and the Song of Songs compares a loved one to a gazelle. It was once widespread but lost much of its habitat to farming and building. Now it is protected, and the Gazelle Valley, a nature park in the middle of Jerusalem, was set aside to keep a herd within the city. Glossary: Mountain gazelle

Golden jackal The country's night chorus תן זהובCanis aureus The golden jackal is a small wild dog, tan with a thick coat, and it is among the most common wild animals in Israel. It eats fruit, small animals, and scraps, and it lives from the hills to the edges of cities. At night, jackals can be heard howling in a group, a sound that can startle visitors. Jackals have increased in number in recent decades, partly because of food left by people. The Bible's story of Samson and the foxes may in fact refer to them. Glossary: Golden jackal

Arabian oryx Brought back from the brink ראם לבןOryx leucoryx The Arabian oryx is a pale antelope with long, straight horns. It was hunted out of the wild in the 20th century. Zoos kept a few animals, and in the 1970s and 1980s their descendants were returned to the Negev and the Arava. A breeding center at Yotvata, the Hai-Bar nature reserve, helped build the herd, and wild herds now live in the desert there. Oryx are well adapted to heat and can go long periods without drinking water. Glossary: Arabian oryx

Wild ass A desert runner returns פראEquus hemionus The wild ass, or onager, is a sandy-colored relative of the donkey that once roamed the region's deserts. It disappeared locally by the early 20th century. In 1982, animals from a related population were released in the Negev. They have bred, and herds can now be seen near Makhtesh Ramon and Sde Boker. Wild asses are fast and shy, and they can run at great speed. Visitors should watch from a distance, since the animals can be aggressive in the breeding season. Glossary: Wild ass

Arabian leopard A shadow in the desert cliffs נמר ערביPanthera pardus nimr The Arabian leopard is a small, pale leopard that survives in remote, rocky canyons of the Judean desert and the Negev. It is extremely rare, and only a handful of animals remain in Israel. The few photographs of it come from motion-triggered cameras set up by researchers. It hunts hyraxes and ibex at night and avoids people. Protecting it is a major conservation effort, and the Nature and Parks Authority monitors the cliffs. Visitors almost never see one. Glossary: Arabian leopard

Striped hyena The shy scavenger צבוע מפוספסHyaena hyaena The striped hyena has a grey coat with dark stripes and a long, bristly mane. It lives in hills and deserts, rests in caves or dens by day, and hunts or scavenges at night. It feeds mostly on carrion, bones, and fruit, and it avoids contact with people. Because it is nocturnal and secretive, few visitors see one, though it is not especially rare. The Bible mentions a place called the Valley of Zeboim, from a Hebrew word that is often linked to the hyena. Glossary: Striped hyena

Fire salamander Black and gold in the rain סלמנדרהSalamandra infraimmaculata The fire salamander is a black amphibian with bright yellow spots. It is the only salamander in Israel, and it lives at the southern edge of its range in the damp woods of the Galilee, the Golan, and the Carmel. Salamanders hide under rocks and logs by day and come out on rainy winter nights to feed and breed in forest pools. Their skin gives off a mild poison that deters predators. They are protected, and their populations depend on seasonal ponds that are drying up. Glossary: Fire salamander

FLORA AND FAUNA Birds of the Land Not every bird is passing through. Many species live in Israel all year, and a visitor who walks through a park, an orchard, or a village will meet several of them. Hawks and falcons also circle over many fields. Hoopoe Israel's national bird דוכיפתUpupa epops The hoopoe is a cinnamon-colored bird with black and white wings and a fan-shaped crest that it raises when excited. It was chosen as Israel's national bird in a public vote in 2008. It has a long, curved bill that it uses to probe lawns and soil for insects. It is common in parks, orchards, and gardens

Hoopoe Israel's national bird דוכיפתUpupa epops The hoopoe is a cinnamon-colored bird with black and white wings and a fan-shaped crest that it raises when excited. It was chosen as Israel's national bird in a public vote in 2008. It has a long, curved bill that it uses to probe lawns and soil for insects. It is common in parks, orchards, and gardens across the country, and it nests in holes in trees and walls. Its soft, three-note call, oop-oop-oop, gives the bird its English name. Glossary: Hoopoe

White-spectacled bulbul The bold garden songbird בולבול מצויPycnonotus xanthopygos The white-spectacled bulbul is a medium-sized songbird with a dark head, pale body, and a yellow patch beneath the tail. It is one of the most common and noisy birds in Israeli gardens, parks, and cafe terraces, and it is bold enough to take crumbs from tables. Bulbuls eat fruit and insects and often build a cup-shaped nest in a bush or balcony. Their cheerful, whistling calls are among the first sounds heard in towns at dawn. Glossary: White-spectacled bulbul

Palestine sunbird A tiny jewel at the flowers צופית ארץ ישראליתCinnyris osea The Palestine sunbird is a tiny, nectar-feeding bird with a long, curved bill. In spring the male shines metallic green and purple, while the female is a plain olive-brown. It hovers briefly or clings to the stem to sip from blossoms such as hibiscus, aloe, and eucalyptus, and it also catches small insects. Sunbirds are common in gardens and wadis from the Galilee to the Dead Sea. The hanging, pouch-like nest is woven from grass and spider silk. Glossary: Palestine sunbird

Griffon vulture A giant of the cliffs נשר מקראיGyps fulvus The griffon vulture is one of the largest birds in Israel, with a wingspan of up to two and a half meters. It nests on cliffs in the Golan, the Judean desert, and the Negev, and it soars for hours on warm air, looking for carcasses. At Gamla, in the Golan, visitors can watch the birds from a lookout. The vulture's Hebrew name, nesher, appears often in the Bible. Griffons are endangered locally, and conservationists feed them and track them with tags. Glossary: Griffon vulture

Barn owl A pale hunter of the night תנשמת לבנהTyto alba The barn owl is a pale, heart-faced owl that hunts silently over fields at night. It eats mostly mice and voles, and it is a valuable ally to farmers. In Israel, farmers have set up thousands of nest boxes across fields and orchards to attract barn owls and reduce chemical poisons for pest control. The program is one of the best-known examples of biological pest control in the world. Barn owls also nest in old buildings and cliffs. They are often heard as a harsh hiss. Glossary: Barn owl

Eurasian jay A colorful bird of the oak woods עורבניGarrulus glandarius The Eurasian jay is a pinkish-brown bird with a flash of bright blue on each wing. It lives in oak and pine woods of the Galilee, the Carmel, and the Judean hills. Jays are noisy and cautious, and they hide acorns in the ground for winter. Many of the acorns are forgotten and sprout, so the jay helps oak forests to spread. It is often heard before it is seen, with a harsh, scratchy call that can carry through the woods. Glossary: Eurasian jay

Dove A bird of Genesis and the city יונהColumba livia The Hebrew word yonah covers the wild rock dove of the cliffs and the city pigeons that descended from it. Doves have lived near people for thousands of years, and they nest on ledges, in cliffs, and on buildings. In Genesis, Noah sends out a dove, and it returns with an olive leaf, a sign that the flood has ended. The dove has since become a symbol of peace in many cultures. In Israel today, doves are common on the streets of every city. Glossary: Dove

Hooded crow Clever and everywhere עורב אפורCorvus cornix The hooded crow has a black head, wings, and tail, and a grey body. It lives in cities, fields, and beaches throughout the country. It is one of the smartest birds in Israel, able to open food containers, use tools, and recognize individual faces. Crows eat nearly anything, from fruit to scraps and carrion. They nest in tall trees, often in noisy colonies. Farmers sometimes dislike them for pulling seedlings, but they also clear away waste and insects. Glossary: Hooded crow

Syrian woodpecker A drummer of the orchards נקר סוריDendrocopos syriacus The Syrian woodpecker is a black-and-white woodpecker with a pinkish-red patch under the tail. It lives in orchards, parks, and villages, where it drills into trees for insects, and it drums on dead branches to claim territory. It nests in holes it digs in tree trunks. The species spread into Israel and nearby lands from the north over the last century, helped by the growth of orchards. Its loud, sharp call is a regular sound in the early morning. Glossary: Syrian woodpecker

Common myna A newcomer from Asia מיינה מצויהAcridotheres tristis The common myna is a brown bird with a bright yellow patch around each eye. It is not native to Israel. Escaped pet birds started a wild population in the 20th century, and since then the species has spread through towns and cities. Mynas are noisy, bold, and aggressive, and they push out other birds from nest holes. For this reason, many consider the myna a pest, and some municipalities try to control it. It remains one of the most visible birds in Israeli cities. Glossary: Common myna

Common kestrel The hovering falcon בז מצויFalco tinnunculus The common kestrel is a small falcon with a rusty back and a grey head in the male. It hunts by hovering in place over a field or roadside, watching for mice and large insects. Some kestrels nest on the ledges of apartment buildings, and in a few towns, people have built nest boxes for them. Many winter visitors join the resident birds in the autumn. In the Hebrew language the bird is called a baz, and its high, fast call, kee-kee-kee, can be heard from rooftops. Glossary: Common kestrel

Long-legged buzzard A hawk of the open hills עקב עיטיButeo rufinus The long-legged buzzard is a large, broad-winged hawk with a pale head and a rusty tail. It soars over hills, fields, and the edge of the desert, hunting mice, lizards, and snakes. It nests on cliffs and in trees, and it is one of the largest hawks that live in the country year-round. In winter, birds from farther north join the resident population. It is often seen perched on a pole beside a road, watching for movement in the grass. Glossary: Long-legged buzzard

FLORA AND FAUNA Migrating Birds Israel sits on one of the world's main bird migration routes, linking Europe and Asia with Africa. Every spring and autumn, hundreds of millions of birds pass over the country. The best places to watch are the Hula Valley, the Golan, Jerusalem, and Eilat. Mediterranean Sea JORDAN EGYPT Common crane Winter guests at the Hula עגור אפורGrus grus The common crane is a tall, grey bird with a black-and-white neck and a red patch on its head. Tens of thousands of cranes spend the winter in the Hula Valley in the north, arriving in the autumn and leaving in the spring.

Common crane Winter guests at the Hula עגור אפורGrus grus The common crane is a tall, grey bird with a black-and-white neck and a red patch on its head. Tens of thousands of cranes spend the winter in the Hula Valley in the north, arriving in the autumn and leaving in the spring. In the past, they ate crops, and so farmers and conservationists agreed to feed them corn at the Agamon Hula park, which keeps them from nearby fields. Visitors watch them at dawn and dusk, when flocks fly out to feed or return to roost. Glossary: Common crane

White stork Spirals over the hills חסידה לבנהCiconia ciconia The white stork is a large white bird with black wing tips and a long red bill. Hundreds of thousands pass through Israel on their way between Europe and Africa each spring and autumn. They are too heavy to flap for long and ride warm air, so they gather in huge, slowly turning spirals and then glide to the next one. Flocks stop overnight in fields and fish ponds. Storks are mentioned in the Bible, and people regard their return in spring as a sign of the season. Glossary: White stork

Great white pelican Giants on the fish ponds שקנאי לבןPelecanus onocrotalus The great white pelican is one of the largest flying birds, with a wingspan of close to three meters. Large flocks pass over Israel in spring and autumn, and many stop to rest on fish ponds, reservoirs, and in the Hula Valley. They fly in formation and glide on warm air. They feed on fish, which has led to conflicts with fish-pond farmers, who scare them away. Some pelicans spend the winter in Israel, and visitors can watch them at the Agamon Hula and at coastal pools. Glossary: Great white pelican

Levant sparrowhawk A flood of small hawks אצבעות-נץ קצרAccipiter brevipes The Levant sparrowhawk is a small, slim hawk with a pale grey back and barred underparts. In spring, thousands pass over Eilat in a single morning, crossing the Gulf of Aqaba on their way from Africa to the Balkans and the Black Sea region. The sight draws bird-watchers from many countries. The hawks travel in loose flocks and feed along the way on lizards, insects, and small birds. In autumn, they return along a similar route, and they are watched near Eilat. Glossary: Levant sparrowhawk

Steppe eagle A giant from the plains of Asia עיט ערבותAquila nipalensis The steppe eagle is a large, dark brown eagle that breeds in the open grasslands of central Asia. Each autumn it flies south to Africa and Arabia, and each spring it returns. Tens of thousands pass over Israel, and the best places to see them are the Arava and Eilat. The eagles ride rising warm air and then glide for long distances. The species is endangered worldwide, in part because of habitat loss and power lines, and counts at Eilat help scientists to follow its numbers. Glossary: Steppe eagle

European honey buzzard A raptor that raids the wasp nest עקב צרעיםPernis apivorus The European honey buzzard is a brown and barred raptor that breeds in European forests. It is a specialist in eating wasps and bees, and it digs up nests and eats the grubs. Hundreds of thousands pass through Israel each autumn on their way to tropical Africa. Huge flocks spiral up on warm air currents and then glide south, in sights that are visible from inland lookouts and along the coast. Counts of the birds in Israel have helped scientists follow European populations. Glossary: European honey buzzard

Macedonian king who conquered the Persian Empire. He took the land in 332 BCE and began the Hellenistic age there, when Greek culture spread through the region.
Immigration of Jews to the land of Israel, from the Hebrew word for "ascent." Historians count successive waves from 1882, starting with the First Aliyah.

Wave of Jewish immigration from 1919 to 1923, about 35,000 people, mostly young pioneers from Eastern Europe after the First World War. They drained swamps, built roads and founded farming villages in the Jezreel Valley.

Sephardic rabbi, 1798 to 1878, who urged Jews to return to the land as a practical first step toward redemption.

Clay tablets of about 1350 BCE from Egypt, letters from Canaanite rulers including the king of Jerusalem asking the pharaoh for help.
Poet, 1924 to 2000, born in Würzburg, who lived in Jerusalem. His first collection, Now and in Other Days, appeared in 1955, and he won the Israel Prize in 1982.
Prophet of the 8th century BCE, a shepherd from Tekoa near Bethlehem, who denounced injustice in the northern kingdom.

Seleucid king from 175 to 164 BCE who banned Jewish practice and defiled the Temple. His decrees led to the Maccabean Revolt.
Coastal site north of Herzliya with Crusader fortifications and traces of earlier Persian and Roman towns. The Mamluks destroyed the fortress in 1265.
Organization of Arab states founded in Cairo in 1945, now with 22 members. The rankings in this book count its members as one bloc.
Arab uprising against British rule and Jewish immigration from 1936 to 1939. It led to the Peel Commission and the White Paper of 1939.
Negev town founded in 1962 beside the ruins of ancient Arad, a Canaanite city and later a fortress of Judah. The Bible mentions it in Numbers 21.
Leader of the Palestine Liberation Organization from 1969 and first head of the Palestinian Authority. He shared the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize.
Painter, 1896 to 1992, born in Galicia, who studied at the Bauhaus under Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky. He settled in Jerusalem in 1933 and directed the Bezalel School from 1940 to 1952.
City in the hills of Samaria founded in 1978, home to Ariel University. It stands on the ridge overlooking the coastal plain.
Hasmonean ruler who in about 104 BCE was the first to take the title of king.
Port city south of Tel Aviv, and today Israel's largest port. In the Bible it was a Philistine stronghold that held the captured Ark of the Covenant.
Coastal city that was a major Philistine port and later a Crusader fortress. Its national park holds a Canaanite arched gate about 3,800 years old.
Empire in northern Mesopotamia that dominated the region in the 9th to 7th centuries BCE. It destroyed Samaria in 722 BCE and Lachish in 701 BCE.
Coastal village south of Haifa. The British ran a detention camp there for illegal Jewish immigrants in the 1930s and 1940s. A raid in 1945 freed about 200 detainees.
Low-level war of 1967 to 1970 between Israel and Egypt along the Suez Canal.
Mathematician born in Frankfurt in 1930 and a professor at the Hebrew University. He shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in economics for his work on game theory and conflict.
Pamphlet of 1882 by Leo Pinsker that argued Jews must seek independence themselves and not wait for others to grant it.
Nabataean city in the Negev on the Incense Route, a UNESCO World Heritage site. Caravans carried frankincense and spices through it.
Ancient city on the Euphrates in today's Iraq. King Nebuchadnezzar took it to the height of its power and destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BCE, deporting its elite.
Return of Jewish exiles to Judea after Cyrus the Greatconquered Babylon in 539 BCE. It led to the rebuilding of the Second Temple.
Letter of 2 November 1917 in which the British government expressed support for a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine.
Springs at the foot of Mount Hermon that feed the Jordan. Greeks and Romans honored the god Pan there, and Caesarea Philippi was built nearby.

Israeli singer who won the 2018 Eurovision Song Contest with the song "Toy."
Swiss city where Theodor Herzl held the First Zionist Congress in 1897.

Hill above the Sea of Galilee where Christian tradition places the Sermon on the Mount.
Largest city of the Negev, where Abrahammade a covenant with Abimelech, according to Genesis 21. A British cavalry charge took it from the Ottomans in 1917.
Israeli prime minister from 1977 to 1983 and former head of the Irgun. He signed the Camp David Accords with Egypt.
Biblical site where Jacob dreamed of a ladder reaching heaven. It was a cult center in the time of the northern kingdom. A modern Israeli community stands nearby.
City at the junction of the Jordan and Jezreel valleys. Its Roman and Byzantine ruins, called Scythopolis, include a theater and bathhouses. It was a city of the Decapolis.
Leader of the Jewish community before independence, who declared the state on 14 May 1948 and was Israel's first prime minister. He retired to Sde Boker in the Negev.
Jerusalem sage who wrote the Wisdom of Ben Sira, also called Sirach, about 180 BCE. The book was written in Hebrew and is part of the Septuagint.

Israeli prime minister from 2021 to 2022, heading a coalition of eight parties.
Town in the lower Galilee with a great Jewish burial ground. Rabbi Judah the Prince was buried there about 220 CE. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Bethlehem is the town south of Jerusalem where David was born and where Christian tradition places the birth of Jesus. Herodium, Herod's palace fortress, lies nearby.
Art school founded in Jerusalem in 1906, the first Jewish art academy in the land. It is now the Bezalel Academy of Arts and Design.

British rule over the land, assigned by the League of Nations and lasting from the 1920s until May 1948.
Wave of destruction about 1200 BCE that ended Egyptian rule in Canaan and toppled many cities of the eastern Mediterranean. The Sea Peoples were part of it.
Makeshift supply road built in the spring of 1948 to bypass the Latrun roadblock and break the siege of Jerusalem.

Two suicide bombings of the No. 18 bus in Jerusalem on 25 February and 3 March 1996 that killed 45 people. Hamas was behind them, and they shook public support for the Oslo Accords before the 1996 election.
The eastern Roman Empire, which ruled the land from the 4th century. It lost it briefly to Persia in 614 and finally to the Arabs in 638.
Port city built by Herod between about 22 and 10 BCE and later the Roman capital of Judea. Its harbor, theater and aqueduct survive.

Village in the lower Galilee where, according to the New Testament, Jesusturned water into wine at a wedding.
Biblical name of the land west of the Jordan before the Israelite settlement, home of the Canaanites.
Peoples of the land before the Israelites, organized in city- states such as Hazor and Megiddo, and known for the early alphabet.
Fishing village on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee where Jesus taught. The ruins include a synagogue of the 4th or 5th century.
Tel Aviv's main open-air market, called the Shuk HaCarmel, in use since the 1920s.
Coastal ridge above Haifa. The Bible places the contest of Elijah with the prophets of Baal there.

Hilltop west of Jerusalem where Israeli forces fought in April 1948 to open the road to the city.

Oldest part of Jerusalem, on the ridge south of the Temple Mount above the Gihon Spring. Hezekiah's tunnel runs under it.
Fertile strip along the Mediterranean from Gaza to Mount Carmel. It holds most of Israel's population and its biggest cities.

European Christian armies who took Jerusalem in 1099 and held parts of the land until the Mamluks took Acre in 1291.
Series of European Christian military campaigns to take Jerusalem, beginning in 1095. The Crusaders ruled parts of the land from 1099 until 1291.

Blood libel of 1840 in Damascus in which Jews were falsely accused of murder. It drew Moses Montefiore and other European Jews into a campaign for their defense.
Israeli singer born in 1972 who won the 1998 Eurovision Song Contest with the song Diva. She was the first openly transgender winner of the contest.
Second king of Israel, about 1000 BCE. According to the Bible he killed Goliath, made Jerusalem his capital and founded a dynasty. Tradition credits him with the Psalms.
Citadel by the Jaffa Gate with remains from the Hasmonean to the Ottoman periods. It is now the museum of the history of Jerusalem. The name comes from a mistaken tradition linking it to David.

Israeli general and politician, 1915 to 1981, who lost an eye fighting in Lebanon in 1941. He was chief of staff during the Suez Crisis, defense minister in the Six-Day War and foreign minister under Menachem Begin.
Salt lake between Israel and Jordan, about 430 meters below sea level, the lowest land on earth. Its level is falling by about a meter a year.
