Mountain north of Shechem, paired with Mount Gerizim. According to Deuteronomy, the curses were pronounced from Ebal.
Neighbor to the southwest. It ruled Canaan in the Bronze Age, fought Israel in 1948, 1956, 1967 and 1973, and signed the first Arab peace treaty with Israel in 1979.
Nazi official who organized the deportation of Jews to the death camps. Israel captured him in Argentina in 1960, tried him in Jerusalem and hanged him in 1962.
Israel's southernmost city, at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba on the Red Sea. It is known for coral reefs and desert resorts.
Oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea with springs and waterfalls. According to 1 Samuel, David hid there from Saul.
Village in the hills southwest of Jerusalem, traditionally the birthplace of John the Baptist. It is now a neighborhood of the city.
Kibbutz in the southern Golan Heightsfounded after 1967 and known for its vineyards.
Israeli singer, 1939 to 2013, whose songs from the 1960s onward made him a leading voice of Israeli pop and rock. Crowds filled Rabin (Kings of Israel) Square to mourn him.
High priest at Shiloh and mentor of the prophet Samuel, according to 1 Samuel.
Prophet of the 9th century BCE who opposed Ahab and Jezebel. He is remembered for the contest with the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel.
Prophet of the 9th century BCE and successor of Elijah, who served in the northern kingdom.
Town in Uganda whose airport was the scene of the Entebbe raidin 1976.
Israeli commando operation of 4 July 1976 that freed hostages held by hijackers at Entebbe Airport in Uganda. The unit's commander, Yonatan Netanyahu, was killed.
Israeli prime minister from 1963 until his death in 1969. He succeeded David Ben-Gurion and formed a national unity government days before the Six-Day War.
Annual European song contest. Netta Barzilai won it for Israel in 2018, and Israel has won four times.
Scribe who, according to tradition, led a group of exiles back from Babylon about 458 BCE and taught the Torah in Jerusalem.
Dynasty of Egyptian caliphs who conquered the land in 969. Seljuk and Crusader advances ended their hold.
Region of northern Israel with hills, valleys and the Sea of Galilee. After 135 CE it became the center of Jewish life, where the Mishnah and Jerusalem Talmudwere written.
Freshwater lake about 21 kilometers long, about 210 meters below sea level, and Israel's main reservoir. Many events of the life of Jesus took place on its shores.
Fortress town in the Golan Heights that fell to the Romans after a siege in 67 CE. Its ruins and a vulture reserve are now a nature park.
Ancient coastal city and Philistine center on the Mediterranean, today the Gaza Strip.
Battle of 1917 in which British forces took Gaza from the Ottomans and opened the way to Jerusalem.
Farming communities within a few kilometers of the Gaza Strip, among them Be'eri, Kfar Aza and Nir Oz. Hamasattacked them on 7 October 2023.
Israel's withdrawal in 2005 from Gaza and from four settlements in northern Samaria. About 8,000 settlers were removed.
Mountain above Shechem, holy to the Samaritans and the place of the blessings in Deuteronomy.
Olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives where, according to the New Testament, Jesus prayed the night before his arrest.
Ancient city on the road between Jerusalem and the coast. According to 1 Kings 9 Solomon fortified it, and archaeologists have found a Solomonic-era gate.
Basalt plateau between the Galilee and Syria. Israel took it in the Six-Day War and applied its law there in 1981.
Poet and children's author, 1911 to 1970, born in Königsberg, who settled in Tel Aviv in 1935. She later taught literature at the Hebrew University.
Philistine warrior from Gath whom the young David killed with a sling, as told in 1 Samuel 17.
Novelist born in Jerusalem in 1954. His books include To the End of the Land, and he won the 2017 Man Booker International Prize for A Horse Walks into a Bar.

Painter, sculptor and author, 1898 to 1980, who came to the land with his family in 1905 and grew up in the new city of Tel Aviv. He illustrated children's books and made mosaics and murals that decorate Tel Aviv.
Hebrew-language theater founded in Moscow in 1917 and settled in Tel Aviv in 1931. It is Israel's national theater.
Roman emperor from 117 to 138 CE. After the Bar Kokhba revolthe refounded Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina and forbade Jews to enter it.
Underground Jewish defense force of the British Mandate, founded in the early 1920s. It formed the core of the Israel Defense Forces in 1948.
Prophet of about 520 BCE who urged the returned exiles to rebuild the Second Temple.
Israel's third largest city, on the slopes of Mount Carmel. It has a major port, the Technion and the Bahai Gardens, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Palestinian Islamist movement founded in 1987 that has ruled Gaza since 2007. Israel, the United States and the European Union list it as a terrorist organization. It led the October 7, 2023 attack.
Eight-day festival of lights that marks the rededication of the Temple in 164 BCE after the Maccabean Revolt.
Pietist movement that began in Eastern Europe in the 18th century. Hasidic Jews settled in Tiberias and Safed in 1777.
Dynasty descended from the Maccabees. They ruled Judea as high priests and later kings from about 140 BCE until Herodtook the throne in 37 BCE.
Israel's national anthem. Its words come from the poem Tikvatenu by Naftali Herz Imber of 1878, and its melody is a folk tune.
Israeli singer, 1957 to 2000, born to a Yemenite Jewish family in Tel Aviv. She placed second at the 1983 Eurovision Song Contestand reached audiences around the world in the 1980s.

Canaanite city in the Upper Galilee. It was the largest fortified city in its region, at its peak from about 1750 BCE. The Bible says Solomon fortified it, and archaeologists have found Solomonic-era gates there.
The Jewish scriptures in three parts, the Torah, the Prophets and the Writings. Christians call it the Old Testament.
Israel's first university, begun on Mount Scopus in 1918 and opened in 1925. Chaim Weizmann and Albert Einstein helped found it.
City in the Judean hills with the Cave of the Patriarchs, the traditional burial place of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the first capital of David's reign.
Spread of Greek language and culture after Alexander the Great. In Judea it divided Jews and led to the Maccabean Revolt.

Highest mountain in the region, 2,814 meters, on the border of Syria and Lebanon. Israel's ski resort lies on its southern slopes, and since December 2024 Israel has held positions on the Syrian side.
Roman client king of Judea from 37 to 4 BCE. He rebuilt the Second Temple and built Caesarea, Masada and Herodium.
Fortress and palace that Herod built on an artificial hill south of Jerusalem. He was buried there according to Josephus.
Biochemist born in Hungary in 1937 who came to Israel as a boy. With Aaron Ciechanover he won the 2004 Nobel Prize in chemistry and worked at the Technion.
Viennese journalist, 1860 to 1904, founder of political Zionism. He convened the First Zionist Congress at Basel in 1897.
Coastal city north of Tel Aviv, founded in 1924 and named for Theodor Herzl. It is a high-tech and diplomatic center.
German Jewish socialist, 1812 to 1875, whose book Rome and Jerusalem of 1862 called for a Jewish state. He is an early voice of Zionism.
Lebanese Shia militia and political party formed in 1982 with Iranian support. It fought Israel in the Second Lebanon War.
King of Judah around 715 to 686 BCE. He strengthened Jerusalem, dug the water tunnel to the Siloam pool, and survived Sennacherib's siege of 701 BCE.
Anatolian empire that clashed with Egypt at Battle of Kadeshabout 1274 BCE.
Nazi Germany's murder of six million Jews in Europe from 1941 to 1945. Israel marks it each year on Yom HaShoah.
Church in the Old City built over the traditional sites of the crucifixion and burial of Jesus. Constantine began it about 335, and the Crusaders rebuilt it.
Prophet of the 8th century BCE in the northern kingdom, shortly before the fall of Samaria.
Polish violinist, 1882 to 1947, who founded the Palestine Symphony Orchestra in 1936. He recruited its players from Jewish musicians who had lost their posts in Europe.
Valley of the upper Jordan in the Galilee, drained in the 1950s and partly restored as a nature reserve. Hundreds of millions of migrating birds pass through it each year.
Synagogue in the Jewish Quarter of the Old City, destroyed in 1948 and rebuilt in 2010. The name means "ruin."
Foreign rulers of northern Egypt from about 1650 to 1550 BCE, many of them Canaanite in origin.

War from 1947 to 1949 that followed the UN Partition Plan and Israel's declaration of independence on 14 May 1948.

Palestinian uprising that began in September 2000 and brought a wave of suicide bombings. It lasted until about 2005.
Country east of Iraq, heir of the Persian Empire. It has been an Islamic republic since 1979 and backs Hezbollah and Hamas. The rankings in this book count it separately from the Arab League.
Modern state in ancient Mesopotamia, home of Babylon and Assyria. It fought Israel in 1948 and 1967 and fired Scud missilesin 1991.
Underground Jewish organization of the Mandate years, led from 1944 by Menachem Begin. It bombed the King David Hotel in 1946.
Israeli air-defense system in use since 2011 that intercepts short-range rockets and shells. It was developed by Rafael Advanced Defense Systems.
Son of Abraham and second of the three patriarchs. By tradition he is buried at Hebron.
Prophet who lived in Jerusalem in the 8th century BCE, a counselor of Hezekiah. The Book of Isaiah is among the most quoted in the Bible.
The Jewish state, declared on 14 May 1948, with Jerusalem as its capital. The name is older. It was given to Jacob and later to the Israelite kingdoms.
Israel's army, navy and air force, formed in May 1948 from the Haganah and other forces. Service is compulsory for most Jewish and Druze citizens.
Jerusalem museum opened in 1965 with collections of archaeology, art and Judaica. It houses the Shrine of the Book.
The descendants of Jacob, the people of the twelve tribes and of the ancient kingdoms of Israel and Judah.
Third patriarch, renamed Israel, whose twelve sons became the tribes. He dreamed of a ladder to heaven at Beit El.
Ancient port south of Tel Aviv, among the oldest in the world. The Bible links it to Jonah and to the timber for Solomon's Temple. It was merged into Tel Aviv in 1950.
Harbor of ancient Jaffa, where cedar logs for Solomon's Temple arrived, according to 2 Chronicles. It is now a gallery and restaurant quarter.
Romanian-born artist, 1895 to 1984, and a founder of the Dada movement in Zurich. He came to the land in 1941 and in 1953 helped start the artists' village of Ein Hod near Mount Carmel.
King of Israel from about 841 to 814 BCE. The Black Obelisk of the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III shows him paying tribute.
Prophet in Jerusalem before and after the Babylonian conquest of 586 BCE who warned of the city's fall.
One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and the lowest on earth, in the Jordan Valley near the Dead Sea.

Capital of Israel and the holiest city of Judaism. King David made it his capital about 1000 BCE and Solomon built the First Temple there. x: Song written by Naomi Shemer and first sung in May 1967. It became a second anthem after the Six-Day War.

Phoenician princess who married Ahab and became queen of Israel. The prophet Elijah opposed her promotion of Baal worship.
Kingdom east of the Jordan River. It held Judea and Samaria and East Jerusalem from 1948 to 1967 and signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1994.

Jewish general in the Galilee who surrendered to Rome and wrote The Jewish War about 75 CE. He is the chief source for the period.
Successor of Moses who led the Israelites across the Jordan, according to the Bible. Tradition places the covenant ceremony at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.
King of Judah from about 640 to 609 BCE who centralized worship in Jerusalem and reformed the faith.
Leader of the Maccabean Revolt after 166 BCE. He retook Jerusalem and rededicated the Temple in 164 BCE, and he fell in battle in 160 BCE.

Southern hill country around Jerusalem, named for the tribe of Judah and the kingdom of Judah. The Romans called the province Judaea.

Central hill country between the Jordan Valley and the coastal plain, the heartland of the ancient kingdoms of Israel and Judah. Israel took it from Jordan in 1967. Hill country west and south of Jerusalem, with villages, kibbutzim and sites from the battles of 1948.
Tradition of Jewish mysticism. Its center in the 16th century was Safed, and its central text is the Zohar.
Ancient city on the Orontes River in Syria. Ramses II and the Hittites fought there in about 1274 BCE.
Clash about 1274 BCE between Ramses II and the Hittites on the Orontes River in Syria. It is one of the earliest battles with a detailed record.
Israeli sculptor and painter, 1932 to 2015. He is known for his paintings of sheep and for Fallen Leaves, a floor of iron faces at the Jewish Museum in Berlin.
Psychologist, 1934 to 2024, born in Tel Aviv and trained at the Hebrew University. He won the 2002 Nobel Prize in economics for work on how people make decisions under uncertainty.
Scholar, 1488 to 1575, who settled in Safed and wrote the Shulchan Aruch, the most widely accepted code of Jewish law.
Town in the Golan Heights founded in 1977. An archaeological park beside it shows a village of the Talmudic era.
Writer of short stories and film scripts, born in Ramat Gan in 1967. His first collection, Pipelines, appeared in 1992, and his stories are widely translated.

Fortified city of Judah southwest of Jerusalem. Sennacherib destroyed it in 701 BCE and showed the siege on the palace reliefs at Nineveh, now in the British Museum.

Hill and monastery on the road to Jerusalem. Israeli attacks to take its police fort failed in May and June 1948, and the Burma Road bypassed it.
Neighbor to the north. Israel fought wars in Lebanon in 1982 and 2006, and Hezbollah is based there.

Cave near the southern shore of the Dead Sea where, according to tradition, Lot and his daughters took refuge after the fall of Sodom and Gomorrah.
Jewish groups formed in Russia and Romania from the 1880s to promote settlement in the land. They supported the First Aliyah.
Attack of 15 May 1974 in which three gunmen of the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine seized a school in the northern town of Ma'alot. Twenty-two schoolchildren were among those killed.
Jewish uprising that began in 167 BCE against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV and his ban on Jewish practice. The Maccabees rededicated the Temple in 164 BCE, an event remembered at Hanukkah.
Family of the priest Mattathias and his sons who led the Maccabean Revolt. Their descendants were the Hasmoneans.
Mosaic floor map of the 6th century in a church at Madaba, Jordan, made between 542 and 570. It is the oldest surviving map of the Holy Land and shows Jerusalem at its center.
Conference of October 1991 that for the first time brought Israel and its Arab neighbors into direct talks.
Fishing town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, home of Mary Magdalene. Excavations in 2009 uncovered a synagogue of the 1st century and the Magdala Stone.
Jerusalem's main open-air market, known as the Shuk, founded in the 1880s.
Largest of the Negev's erosion craters, about 40 kilometers long and up to 9 kilometers wide.
Slave-soldier dynasty that ruled Egypt and Syria. They defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260 and ruled the land until 1517.
Lithuanian Hebrew writer, 1808 to 1867, whose novel Ahavat Zion (1853) set a love story in the time of Isaiah and is counted the first modern Hebrew novel.
Mountain fortress above the Dead Sea built by Herod. It was the last stronghold of the Jewish revolt against Rome and fell in 73 or 74 CE.
Neighborhood of Jerusalem founded in 1874 and now home to ultra-Orthodox Jews who keep the customs of Eastern Europe.
Ancient mound that guarded a pass between the coastal plain and the Jezreel Valley. It has some twenty layers of city ruins and gave its name to Armageddon. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

Arab trading people whose kingdom, centered on Petra in present-day Jordan, grew rich from the incense and spice caravans that crossed the Negev to the Mediterranean. Jewish sect of the Second Temple period that, according to Josephus and other ancient writers, lived in strict communities, shared property and stressed ritual purity. Many scholars link them to the settlement at Qumran and the Dead Sea Scrolls, though others dispute the connection. They vanish from the record after the revolt against Rome.

Jewish movement of the Second Temple period that stressed study and the oral law alongside the written Torah. Their teachers shaped the Mishnah. After the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE their approach became the basis of rabbinic Judaism. Josephus and the New Testament describe them as a leading party with wide popular support.

Priestly and aristocratic party of the Second Temple period that accepted only the written Torah and rejected the oral law. They were tied to the Temple and its priesthood, and the party faded after the Temple was destroyed in 70 CE.

Name given to Jewish rebel factions in the revolt against Rome of 66 to 73 CE, known as the First Revolt. Groups inside Jerusalem fought each other as well as the Romans. The Sicarii, a separate group, held Masada until its fall. The main source on all of them is Josephus, who opposed the rebellion.

Council of Jewish sages and judges that served as the highest court and legislature of Jewish life. It sat in Jerusalem in the Second Temple period. After 70 CE it was re-formed at Yavne, later moved to the Galilee, and ended about 425 CE.

Jewish communities living outside the land of Israel. It began with the exile to Babylon in 586 BCE and grew after the Roman destruction of Jerusalem. For some two thousand years Jews lived in Babylonia, Egypt, Europe, North Africa and the Americas, while a Jewish presence continued in the land. Today roughly as many Jews live outside Israel as in it.

Dynasty of caliphs that overthrew the Umayyads in 750 and ruled from Baghdad. The land was a frontier province, and by the 10th century Egyptian dynasties controlled it, until the Fatimids conquered it in 969.

Hebrew word for settlement, used for the organized Jewish community in the land before the state of 1948. League of ten Greek-speaking cities of the Roman era, mostly east of the Jordan River in present-day Jordan and Syria. Beit She'an, then called Scythopolis, was the only one west of the river. The cities shared Greek culture and had a measure of self-rule under Rome.
